{{Short description|How data on crime is measured and reported}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=March 2020}}{{Use British English|date=July 2013}}

[[File:CSEW vs PRC trends.svg|alt=Chart showing trend lines for totals of CSEW and PRC compared to those excluding violent crime.|left|thumb|Comparison of trends in UK crime statistics between 2002 and 2022]]
'''Crime statistics in the United Kingdom''' refers to the way crime data is collected and reported in [[England and Wales]], [[Scotland]] and [[Northern Ireland]], which each operate separate judicial systems.

''For information'' ''about UK crime itself, see [[Crime in the United Kingdom]].''

The [[Home Office]] has historical data on individual offences recorded by the police from 1898. A marked increase starting in the late 1950s and accelerating through to the 1980s  led to the question of whether increases were due to changes in how crime was recorded, together with the public's growing willingness to report it. Occasional updates to police counting rules were made in the past, but the first systematic efforts to record crime consistently across all forces in the UK took place in the late 1990s against a backdrop of generally declining crime rates both nationally and [[Crime drop|around the world]].

Today, there are two primary sources of statistics on crime in the UK: Police Recorded Crime ('''PRC''') statistics collected by each regional force, and [[Victim study|victim surveys]] - principally the [[Crime Survey for England and Wales]] ('''CSEW'''), with data from 1981. The CSEW is considered the preferred source for understanding longer-term crime prevalence and genuine trends across the population, while PRC is used to supplement weaknesses in its methodology for high-harm crimes.

While PRC statistics in England and Wales can be directly compared to those of Northern Ireland, they cannot be compared to that of Scotland due to the way Scottish counting rules operate.

The history of PRC statistics in the UK since the late 1990s is fundamentally that of administrative failure followed by statistical recovery. This created a dramatic, but misleading, apparent increase in police reported crime against a steady decrease in surveyed rates, both in the UK and internationally. In particular, the rise from 2002 and the surge from 4 million recorded crimes in the year ending March 2014 to 6.7 million in 2024 in England and Wales, are overwhelmingly methodological in origin. The sharpest periods of this inflation (2002-2004 and 2015–2019) also correlate directly with efforts to enforce data quality and police compliance. Since 2014, while police-reported crime statistics are no longer officially '[[Office for National Statistics|national statistics]]', efforts to bring them up to a sufficient quality to be so are on-going.

Recent changes in police reporting have also depressed positive outcome statistics as crime volumes have risen, compounding a generally negative popular perception of crime rates. Reporting improvements and changes also make direct international comparisons of crime volumes unreliable, particularly for non-homicide violent crime.

== Measurement and publication ==
{{See also|Police National Computer}}

=== Modern police recorded crime statistics ===
An important distinction within police-recorded crime in the UK is made between '[[notifiable offence]]s' recorded according to the National Crime Recording Standard (NCRS), and police 'incidents' (non-crime). Incidents are recorded according to the National Standard for Incident Recording (NSIR) standards using the 'National Incident Category List' to provide uniformity about how the police record an incident and an opportunity to find any incidents that require recording as a [[notifiable offence]]. In 2011, 80% of calls to the police were about incidents specified on the 'National Incident Category List'.<ref>{{Cite web |title=National standard for incident recording counting rules |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-national-standard-for-incident-recording-nsir-counting-rules |access-date=2025-11-19 |website=GOV.UK |language=en}}</ref>

Notifiable offences constitute official police crime statistics, while non-crime incidents are primarily used internally by police for the purposes of resource allocation, intelligence or local reporting.<ref name=":2" /> Incidents are also not to be confused with '[[recordable offence]]s', of which the police must keep records of the conviction/offender on the [[Police National Computer]] (PNC). However, while offences can be recordable, they may also not be notifiable. If so, they are excluded from official crime statistics.<ref name=":10" /> Police forces in the UK record large amounts of information internally, which often includes incidents that are not classified as either notifiable offences or recordable offences.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-11-25 |title=Police Activity Survey |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/police-activity-survey/police-activity-survey |access-date=2025-11-27 |website=GOV.UK |language=en}}</ref>

==== England and Wales ====
[[File:ONS main building, Drummond Gate, London SW1.jpg|alt=Photo of the outside of the building|thumb|Office for National Statistics main building, Drummond Gate, London SW1.]]
The [[Office for National Statistics|Office of National Statistics]] (ONS) is the primary body responsible for publishing crime statistics for England and Wales, using data from both police reported crime and the [[Crime Survey for England and Wales]] (CSEW).

The [[Home Office]] is responsible for collecting and validating police recorded crime data from the 43 territorial police forces of England and Wales and the [[British Transport Police]], and supplies this data to the ONS for compilation and publication.

Three other independent bodies are involved in regulation and quality assurance: [[His Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services]] (HMICFRS) inspects the integrity of police recorded crime data for forces in England and Wales, auditing it with the [[National Crime Recording Standards (England and Wales)|National Crime Recording Standard]] (NCRS) and [[National Standard for Incident Recording (England and Wales)|National Incident Recording Standard]] (NIRS). The [[UK Statistics Authority]] (UKSA) and [[Office for Statistics Regulation]] (OSR) are responsible for promoting and safeguarding the production and publication of official statistics. The OSR also assesses whether statistics meet the standards of the Code of Practice for Statistics, which determines if they can be designated as [[National Statistics]].

In recent years, crime statistics have been made available online in various ways, for example through the Policing Services and Information website, and the London [[Metropolitan Police]]s Stats and Data website. Various third party sites that analyse and re-publish these figures are also available.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Police.UK |url=https://www.police.uk/ |access-date=2025-11-10 |website=www.police.uk |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Stats and data |url=https://www.met.police.uk/police-forces/metropolitan-police/areas/stats-and-data/stats-and-data/ |access-date=2025-11-10 |website=www.met.police.uk |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=England Crime Statistics |url=https://crimerate.co.uk/england |access-date=2025-11-10 |website=CrimeRate}}</ref>

==== Scotland and Northern Ireland ====
[[Scots criminal law]] is separate to English criminal law, including the use of a [[not proven]] verdict at criminal trials in the [[Courts of Scotland]]. The [[Scottish criminal law#List of offences|list of offences]] is also different from England and Wales, and in Northern Ireland.

Crime statistics  are collected and published separately by their respective government bodies (the [[Scottish Government]] and [[Department of Justice (Northern Ireland)|Department of Justice]] in Northern Ireland), though they are also official statistics for those nations.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |date=2025-11-05 |title=User guide to crime statistics for England and Wales: March 2025 |url=https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/crimeandjustice/methodologies/userguidetocrimestatisticsforenglandandwales |access-date=2025-11-10 |website=Office for National Statistics}}</ref>

=== Crime surveys ===

==== England and Wales ====
Since 1982, the [[Crime Survey for England and Wales]] (CSEW) is an attempt to measure both the amount of crime and the impact of crime on England and Wales. These surveys collect information about the victims of crime, the circumstances surrounding the offence and the behaviour of the perpetrators. They are used to plan and measure the results of crime reduction or perception measures. In addition, they collect data about the perception of issues such as [[antisocial behaviour]] and the criminal justice system.<ref name="BCS">{{cite web |date=2009 |title=British Crime Survey and other surveys |url=http://www.homeoffice.gov.uk/rds/bcs1.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100208002602/http://www.homeoffice.gov.uk/rds/bcs1.html |archive-date=8 February 2010 |access-date=24 January 2010 |work=Research Development Statistics |publisher=The Home Office}}</ref>

Other crime surveys include the Commercial Victimisation Survey, which covers small and medium-sized businesses,<ref name="BCS" /> and the Offending, Crime and Justice Survey, with a particular focus on young people.<ref>{{cite web |date=2009 |title=Offending, Crime and justice Survey |url=http://www.homeoffice.gov.uk/rds/offending_survey.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091207130109/http://www.homeoffice.gov.uk/rds/offending_survey.html |archive-date=7 December 2009 |access-date=24 January 2010 |work=Research Development Statistics |publisher=The Home Office}}</ref>

===== Limitations =====
{{Excerpt|Crime Survey for England and Wales#Limitations}}

=== Scotland and Northern Ireland ===
Police recorded crime statistics in [[Scotland]] are collected according to [[Scots law]] on the basis of the Scottish Crime Recording Standard (SCRS), introduced in 2004. Crime statistics for [[England and Wales]] are not directly comparable with those in Scotland<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-07-06 |title=User Guide to Recorded Crime Statistics in Scotland - Comparability across the UK |url=https://www.gov.scot/publications/user-guide-recorded-crime-statistics-scotland-3/pages/24/ |access-date=2025-12-02 |website=Scottish Government |language=en}}</ref> due to the SCRS following a practice called 'subsuming.' This generally means a single incident can be recorded as multiple crimes if different crimes occurred during a continuous action.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2014-01-29 |title=Question reference: S4W-19425 |url=https://www.parliament.scot/chamber-and-committees/questions-and-answers/question?ref=S4W-19425 |access-date=2025-12-02 |website=The Scottish Parliament |language=en}}</ref> In England and Wales, only the most serious crime is counted for statistical purposes (known as the "Principal Crime Rule").

The practice of 'subsuming', and other differences between the SCRS and the NCRS means crime statistics between Scotland and England and Wales are not directly comparable.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-06-24 |title=Recorded Crime in Scotland, 2024-25 - Data and methodology |url=https://www.gov.scot/publications/recorded-crime-scotland-2024-25/pages/data-and-methodology/ |access-date=2025-12-02 |website=Scottish Government |language=en}}</ref>

The legal system in [[Northern Ireland]] is based on that of England and Wales, and the [[Police Service of Northern Ireland|Police Service for Northern Ireland]] (PSNI) has the same notifiable offence list for recorded crime as used in England and Wales. In addition, the PSNI has adopted the National Crime Reporting Standards and [[Home Office]] Counting Rules for recorded crime that apply in England and Wales.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Scottish Crime Recording Board |url=https://www.gov.scot/groups/scottish-crime-recording-board/ |access-date=2025-12-02 |website=Scottish Government |language=en}}</ref>

The [[Scottish Crime and Justice Survey]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Scottish Crime and Justice Survey |url=https://www.gov.scot/collections/scottish-crime-and-justice-survey/ |access-date=2025-12-02 |website=www.gov.scot |language=en}}</ref> and [[Northern Ireland Crime Survey]] have similar purposes to the [[Crime Survey for England and Wales|CSEW]].

=== Other sources of data ===
Various sources of supplementary data on crime and crime outcomes are also available. These are used to compare, validate and predict trends in various types of crime.

Examples include [[National Health Service|NHS]] admissions data for 'sharp objects', using the ICD-10 cause code X99 for 'assault by sharp object", recorded since 2017.<ref name=":17">{{Cite web|title=Crime in England and Wales: Other related tables|url=https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/crimeandjustice/datasets/crimeinenglandandwalesotherrelatedtables|website=Office for National Statistics|access-date=2025-11-30|date=2024-07-24}}</ref> This is compiled from Finished Admission Episodes (FAEs) within NHS hospitals in England and Wales, and is broken down by age group, gender, police force, and ethnicity.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Hospital admissions for assault by sharp objects April 2025|url=https://digital.nhs.uk/supplementary-information/2025/hospital-admissions-for-assault-by-sharp-objects-april-2025|access-date=2025-11-30|website=NHS England Digital|language=en}}</ref> These figures are often quoted by the ONS in relation to statistics on knife crime.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Crime in England and Wales|url=https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/crimeandjustice/bulletins/crimeinenglandandwales/yearendingjune2025|website=Office for National Statistics|access-date=2025-11-30|date=2025-10-23}}</ref>

Police outcomes can be analysed from criminal justice statistics to see how police deal with crimes, such as with arrests, cautions, and other out-of-court disposals. Data is collected on defendants prosecuted, offenders convicted, and remand decisions as well as the types of sentences handed out by courts.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-10-23|title=Criminal justice statistics|url=https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/criminal-justice-statistics|access-date=2025-11-30|website=GOV.UK|language=en}}</ref>

Specialist agencies also gather information on specific areas of crime. For example, the [[National Fraud Intelligence Bureau]] (NFIB) collates fraud data from Report Fraud (the national fraud reporting centre that records incidents of fraud directly from the public and organisations), [[Cifas]] (a UK-wide fraud and financial crime prevention service) and [[UK Finance]] (which collects information on fraud from the card payments industry in the UK).<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-07-25|title=Guide to finding crime statistics|url=https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/crimeandjustice/methodologies/guidetofindingcrimestatisticsoct2016|access-date=2025-11-30|website=Office for National Statistics}}</ref>

== History of changes to counting rules ==

=== Overview ===
There have been distinct phases of discontinuity in police recorded crime statistics in the UK:

# 1898 to twentieth century - Reliant mainly on reports by the public, with variations between regional forces using occasionally updated but poorly-enforced counting rules.
# 1950s onwards - Marked increases in crime accelerating through subsequent decades, leading to questions about these rises and the establishment of the Birish Crime Survey (now the [[Crime Survey for England and Wales]]) in 1982.
# 1998 - A review of counting rules provided greater guidance on crime recording, which in turn produced a rise in the number of many offences while trends in the CSEW moved consistently downward.
# 2002 - Introduction of the [[National Crime Recording Standards (England and Wales)|National Crime Recording Standard]] (NCRS): This mandatory introduction of victim-centric recording created a discrete step-change, initially estimated at 23% inflation for violence categories.
# 2015 - 2019 integrity correction: The longest and largest period of inflation; the loss of 'national statistics' accreditation and the ensuing mandatory police compliance following the exposure of 20% institutional under-recording.<ref>{{Cite news |last= |first= |last2= |first2= |date=2014-05-01 |title=UK police failing to record 20% of crime |url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2014/may/01/uk-police-failing-record-20-percent-crime-report |access-date=2025-11-10 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=}}</ref>
# 2020 onwards - Continuous, granular adjustments to counting rules bringing about both inflation and deflation within specific categories, tending to mask a stable underlying prevalence.

=== History ===
[[File:UK historical crime data 1868-2003.svg|thumb|Recorded offences per 100,000 people in England and Wales during the twentieth century.<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal |last=Dar |first=Aliyah |last2=Thompson |first2=Gavin |last3=Taylor |first3=Mark |last4=Hawkins |first4=Oliver |date=2025-09-11 |title=Olympic Britain |url=https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/rp12-38/ |journal=Research Briefings |language=en-GB |via=House of Commons Library}}</ref>]]
[[File:Birmingham City Police - Criminal record card with drawing of tattoos.jpg|thumb|A criminal record card showing drawings of tattoos. [[Birmingham City Police]], [[West Midlands Police Museum]], c.1910.]]See also [[#Timeline|Timeline]]

For the first half of the twentieth century, official crime statistics in England and Wales were low. During the first two decades of the century, police recorded an average of only 90,000 indictable offences each year - approximately 250 crimes per 100,000 people in 1901.<ref name=":7" /> Officers had considerable autonomy, having originally been given discretion in whether they thought a crime had been committed or not.<ref>{{Cite web |last=|first=|date=1939-11-22|title='Instructions respecting the Duties and Powers of Constables'|url=https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/education/resources/crime-and-punishment-robert-peel/source-one-instructions-respecting-the-duties-and-powers-of-constables/|access-date=2025-11-26|website=The National Archives|language=en-GB}}</ref> Crime later began a steep rise, with an average of over one million crimes recorded each year in the 1960s, increasing to two million during the 1970s, and 3.5m in the 1980s.<ref name=":13">{{Cite web |title=Crimes of the century |url=https://www.parliament.uk/business/publications/research/olympic-britain/crime-and-defence/crimes-of-the-century/ |access-date=2025-11-26 |website=www.parliament.uk |language=en}}</ref> 

Various factors contributed to the increases: changes to the types of offences recorded as crime,<ref name=":14" /> how they were counted, the [[Dark figure of crime|behaviour of the public]] in reporting crimes to the police, and social change. For example, the relatively recent need to inform the police in order to make an insurance claim for burglary; new technologies creating new opportunities for misdemeanours; a growth in the value of ordinary people's personal property, and the criminalisation of drug use.<ref name=":13" />

Since the [[Victorian era]], offences have been rooted in statutes, such as the [[Offences Against the Person Act 1861|Offences against the Person Act 1861]], which defined the categories of serious crime that formed the basis of the national statistical series. But counting rules themselves were not sufficiently detailed, and there was a lack of consistency. Little distinction was made between similar types of crimes, and few examples available to illustrate how the rules should be implemented. This could result in the same offence being recorded as a different crime within and between police forces. Prior to 1998, there was also no policy on new and changing offence types introduced through new legislation.<ref name=":8" />

Because of its severity, homicide receives consistent recording across all jurisdictions and time periods,<ref name=":6" /> thereby minimising officer discretion. But throughout the period of late twentieth century rises, homicide did not show the same degree of increase (roughly 156% from 1960 compared to over 450% for aggregated crime).<ref name=":14" /> 
[[File:Homicide in England and Wales 1898 - 1997.svg|left|thumb|Recorded homicides per 100,000 people in England and Wales 1898 - 1997.<ref name=":14">{{Cite web |date=2016-04-21 |title=Historical crime data |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/historical-crime-data |access-date=2025-11-26 |website=GOV.UK |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-07-06 |title=UK Population Estimates 1851 to 2014 |url=https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/adhocs/004356ukpopulationestimates1851to2014 |access-date=2025-11-26 |website=Office for National Statistics}}</ref>]]
By the late 1970s and early 1980s, the unreliability of police-recorded crime statistics had evolved into an institutional crisis within the [[Home Office]]. The government response was to create a parallel statistical measure independent of law enforcement activity. The launch of the first British Crime Survey (BCS) launched in 1982 (later the [[Crime Survey for England and Wales]]) was explicitly aimed at addressing this acknowledged 'crisis' in official statistics.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Molina |first=Julian |date=2023-11-08 |title=Criminology’s Data: The Home Office and the First British Crime Survey |url=https://thebscblog.wordpress.com/2023/11/08/criminologys-data-the-home-office-and-the-first-british-crime-survey/ |access-date=2025-11-26 |website=The BSC Blog |language=en}}</ref> By 1998, data from the BCS suggested that the police received reports for less than half of all offences that occurred.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Criminal Statistics, England and Wales, 1998 {{!}} Office of Justice Programs |url=https://www.ojp.gov/ncjrs/virtual-library/abstracts/criminal-statistics-england-and-wales-1998 |access-date=2025-11-26 |website=www.ojp.gov}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Crime Survey for England & Wales |url=https://www.crimesurvey.co.uk/en/AboutTheSurvey.html |access-date=2025-11-26 |website=www.crimesurvey.co.uk}}</ref>

==== The National Crime Recording Standard ====
The [[Home Office]] Counting Rules (HOCR) had existed in some form since the 1920s, with processes for determining how police forces record notifiable offence statistics.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-10-15 |title=Crime in England and Wales |url=https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/crimeandjustice/bulletins/crimeinenglandandwales/2015-10-15#accuracy-of-the-statistics |access-date=2025-11-19 |website=Office for National Statistics}}</ref> Until the late 1990s, crime figures for varying crime types were not released to the general public at individual police force level. The annual publication 'Crime in England & Wales' produced by the Home Office began to break the figures down to a smaller area in 1996.<ref>{{cite web |title=Notifiable Offences England and Wales 1996 |url=http://www.homeoffice.gov.uk/rds/pdfs/hosb397.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091212015732/http://www.homeoffice.gov.uk/rds/pdfs/hosb397.pdf |archive-date=12 December 2009 |accessdate=13 December 2011}}</ref>

Following the 1997 General Election, a review of crime statistics<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=1997-10-02 |title=Crime Figures Framework Will Lead To Greater Clarity - Straw |url=https://www.lgcplus.com/archive/crime-figures-framework-will-lead-to-greater-clarity-straw-02-10-1997/ |access-date=2025-11-26 |website=Local Government Chronicle |language=en}}</ref> promised by the then Labour government led to significant changes in crime counting rules and coverage. Taking effect from 1 April 1998,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Keenan |first=Caroline |title=Great Expectations: Changes to the Recording of Crime |url=https://www.radstats.org.uk/no073/review2.htm |access-date=2025-11-27 |website=Radical Statistics}}</ref> these changes immediately resulted in a 14% increase in recorded offences overall, albeit it with a very uneven effect on classifications. Together with a move from the calendar year to the financial year, these reforms created the first major discontinuity in the PRC time series in recent history.<ref name=":8">{{Cite web |last=Gavin |first=Berman |date=2008-10-31 |title=Changes in crime recording practices |url=https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/sn02607/ |access-date=2025-11-05 |website=House of Commons Library}}</ref>

|}{{Anchor|no-criming}}The introduction of the National Crime Recording Standards (England and Wales) (NCRS) in April 2002 marked the first major improvement in the consistency of crime recording across all 43 police forces in England and Wales, and is the reason crime figures before and after that date are generally not directly comparable.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-10-24 |title=Crime in England and Wales: year ending June 2024 |url=https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/crimeandjustice/bulletins/crimeinenglandandwales/yearendingjune2024 |access-date=2025-11-10 |website=Office for National Statistics}}</ref>

One issue subsequently identified was 'no-criming' ('cancellations')<ref>{{Cite web|title=Home Office Crime Recording Rules for frontline officers and staff|url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/counting-rules-for-recorded-crime|website=GOV.UK|date=2025-04-04|access-date=2025-11-30|language=en}}</ref> - the practice of writing off reported notifiable offences from police force statistics as it appeared the NCRS was also applied inconsistently across crimes and regions, and frequently incorrectly:<ref name="justice">{{Cite news |title=Victims let down by poor crime-recording |url=http://www.justiceinspectorates.gov.uk:80/hmic/news/news-feed/victims-let-down-by-poor-crime-recording/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170401173442/http://www.justiceinspectorates.gov.uk:80/hmic/news/news-feed/victims-let-down-by-poor-crime-recording/ |archive-date=2017-04-01 |access-date=2025-11-09 |work=HMIC |language=en-GB}}</ref> in the year to March 2011, 2% of reported rapes in [[Gloucestershire]] were recorded as 'no crime', while 30% of reported rapes in [[Kent]] were so classified.<ref>{{cite web |title=Rape crime figure differences revealed |website=[[BBC News]] |date=9 September 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221213172655/https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-14844985 |archive-date=2022-12-13 |url-status=live |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-14844985}}</ref> This was sometimes due to pressure from performance and other factors.<ref name="justice" />

During the period November 2012 - October 2013, an average of 19% of crimes reported to the police were not recorded.<ref group="Note">There are five reasons for no-criming: the notifiable offence passed to another police force that had jurisdiction for investigation and recording; verifiable information existed that a notifiable offence was not committed; a duplicate record existed of a notifiable offence; a notifiable offence was recorded in error; or an assault when evidence shows it was committed in self-defence.</ref> One quarter of sexual crimes and one-third of violent crimes were ignored by police, with rape being particularly affected with 37% designated as 'no-crime'. Reporting was also inconsistent across local forces.<ref name="justice" /> The failure to properly record crime was called 'inexcusably poor' and 'indefensible' by [[His Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services|Her Majesty's Chief Inspector of Constabulary]] [[Tom Winsor]]. 20% of reviewed decisions to cancel a report were found to be incorrect, and in about a quarter of cases there was no record of victims being informed that their report had been cancelled.<ref name="justice" /> Senior members of the policing establishment admitted to long-term, widespread 'fiddling' of figures, such as [[John Stevens, Baron Stevens of Kirkwhelpington|John Stevens]], former head of the [[Metropolitan Police Service]]:<blockquote>''<nowiki/>'Ever since I’ve been in police service there has been a fiddling of figures. I remember being a detective constable where we used to write off crimes'<ref>{{cite news |title=Lord Stevens admits police have been 'fiddling' crime figures for years |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/crime/10557155/Lord-Stevens-admits-police-have-been-fiddling-crime-figures-for-years.html |work=The Telegraph}}</ref>''</blockquote>{{Anchor|sex-crime}}[[File:UK police recorded sexual offenses 2003-2022.svg|left|thumb|A sharp increase in sex crimes from Oct 2012 marks the start of [[Operation Yewtree]], following the highly publicised [[Jimmy Savile sexual abuse scandal|Jimmy Savile investigations]] and an increased willingness of victims to come forward.<ref name=":12">{{Cite web |date=2023-03-23 |title=Sexual offences in England and Wales overview |url=https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/crimeandjustice/bulletins/sexualoffencesinenglandandwalesoverview/march2022 |access-date=2025-11-19 |website=Office for National Statistics}}</ref>|alt=Line chart showing the rise.]]
In April 2013, the framework for reporting of official police statistics was amended to address these issues.<ref name="HOSB 06162">{{cite web|url=https://www.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/539447/crime-outcomes-hosb0616.pdf|title=Crime outcomes in England and Wales: year ending March 2016|date=July 2016|website=gov.uk|publisher=Home Office|access-date=25 June 2017}}</ref> The [[Home Office]] delegated the responsibility for auditing a police force's compliance with the National Crime Recording Standard (NCRS) to Her Majesty's Chief Inspectorate of Constabulary, later renamed [[His Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services|Her Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire Rescue Service]] (HMICFRS).<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=https://www.justiceinspectorates.gov.uk/hmicfrs/wp-content/uploads/crime-recording-making-the-victim-count.pdf|title=Crime Recording: Making Victims Count|last=Her Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary|date=2014|website=HMICFRS|access-date=23 May 2018}}</ref> The first statistics using  the new framework were published in July 2014.<ref name="HOSB 06162" />

The NCRS mandated that if a victim reported an incident and a police officer, based on the balance of probability, believed a crime had occurred, it must be recorded. This lowered the recording threshold, particularly for violent crime and especially assaults. Police began recording many minor or common assaults (violence with minimal or no injury) that had previously been screened out. This created a large increase in the recorded rate for 'violence against the person.' Recording of sexual assault and rape also improved significantly.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |date=2024-07-24 |title=Exploring diverging trends between the Crime Survey for England and Wales and police recorded crime |url=https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/crimeandjustice/methodologies/exploringdivergingtrendsbetweenthecrimesurveyforenglandandwalesandpolicerecordedcrime |access-date=2025-11-03 |website=Office for National Statistics}}</ref>

An initial analysis estimated the effect of these changes was an increase of 23% in 'violence against the person' offences in the first 12 months of implementation.<ref name=":3" /> While this figure suggested a very large increase in violence, detailed analysis indicated that once recording changes were accounted for, the genuine underlying increase in police recorded violence in that period was approximately 2%.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Jon Simmons,  Tricia Dodd |date=2003-07-01 |title=Crime in England and Wales 2002/2003 |url=https://www.ojp.gov/ncjrs/virtual-library/abstracts/crime-england-and-wales-20022003 |access-date=2025-11-10 |website=Office of Justice Programs}}</ref>

==== The National Standard for Incident Recording ====
'[[Notifiable offence]]s' constitute official police crime statistics, while non-crime 'incidents' are primarily used internally by police for the purposes of resource allocation, intelligence or local reporting. Incidents are recorded according to the National Standard for Incident Recording (NSIR) standards.<ref>{{Cite web|title=National standard for incident recording counting rules|url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-national-standard-for-incident-recording-nsir-counting-rules|website=GOV.UK|access-date=2025-11-30|language=en|date=2011-04-11}}</ref><ref group="Note">The five purposes for the NSIR are to provide uniformity about how the police record an incident; to ensure the correct response to an incident reported to the police; to allow a risk assessment about the incident, particularly considering any threats to safety, identifying vulnerable people, and repeat victims; an opportunity to find any incidents that required recording as a notifiable offence, and to provide management and performance data for use at both a local and national level.</ref> Many incidents reported to the police (like noise complaints or lost property) are not crimes and therefore will never become a notifiable offence, but others may be determined to be crimes later on.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |date=2013-10-23 |title=Collection and recording |url=https://www.college.police.uk/app/information-management/management-police-information/collection-and-recording |access-date=2025-11-19 |website=The College of Policing |language=en}}</ref>

In 2012, [[Her Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services|Her Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary]] audited several police forces about how they recorded incidents and reported that they lacked consistency. It was concerned about the adequacy and quality of the data, especially in identifying vulnerable and repeat victims, particularly in relation to [[anti-social behaviour]] incidents.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Her Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary |date=2012 |title=The Crime Scene: A Review of Police Crime and Incident Reports |url=https://www.justiceinspectorates.gov.uk/hmicfrs/publications/review-police-crime-incident-reports-20120125/ |access-date=24 May 2018 |website=HMICFRS}}</ref>

[[His Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services|HMICFRS]] annually complete a ‘PEEL Assessment’ for each English and Welsh police force. The assessment reviews a force's effectiveness, efficiency, and legitimacy. Each force is graded either as either outstanding, good, requires improvement, or inadequate. The NSIR are still used, but how it complies with the aims of the standards are incorporated into the PEEL Assessment, by for example, how it uses information to identify repeat victims, vulnerable people, and to improve the  management and performance by the police force.<ref>{{Cite news |title=How We Inspect |url=https://www.justiceinspectorates.gov.uk/hmicfrs/peel-assessments/how-we-inspect/ |access-date=25 May 2018 |work=HMICFRS |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |title=PEEL Assessment 2017 |url=https://www.justiceinspectorates.gov.uk/hmicfrs/peel-assessments/peel-2017/ |access-date=25 May 2018 |work=HMICFRS |language=en-GB}}</ref>

==== 2015 - 2019 integrity correction ====
A second significant, but more gradual inflation in police recorded crime numbers occurred following an official inspection and highly critical report by [[Her Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary|HMICFRS]] on the integrity of police crime recording in 2014.<ref name=":4" /> The report found that an estimated 19% of reported notifiable offences were still not being recorded correctly. This led to a subsequent (and ongoing) drive to improve compliance with the NCRS principles. As forces corrected previous under-recording errors, a further sharp increase in recorded crime occurred from around 2014 onwards, particularly for high-volume crimes like violence and sexual offences. The total volume of recorded crime then rose form from 4 million in March 2014 to 6.7 million by 2024.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-07-24 |title=Crime in England and Wales: year ending March 2024 |url=https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/crimeandjustice/bulletins/crimeinenglandandwales/yearendingmarch2024 |access-date=2025-11-10 |website=Office for National Statistics}}</ref> {{Anchor|trends}}[[File:CSEW vs PRC trends.svg|alt=Chart showing trend lines for totals of CSEW and PRC compared to those excluding violent crime.|thumb|350x350px|Surveyed and PRC numbers diverged in the year ending March 2015, while non-violent PRC can be seen mostly to follow the surveyed trend.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-07-24 |title=Exploring diverging trends between the Crime Survey for England and Wales and police recorded crime |url=https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/crimeandjustice/methodologies/exploringdivergingtrendsbetweenthecrimesurveyforenglandandwalesandpolicerecordedcrime |access-date=2025-11-19 |website=Office for National Statistics}}</ref>]]

The period between 2015 and 2019 marks the most significant analytical divergence between the two key statistical series of PRC and victim surveyed trends. The [[Crime Survey for England and Wales]] (CSEW) generally continued to show a decrease in overall crime prevalence, while the police-recorded crime series saw sharp rises with volumes eventually surpassing the number of reported CSEW incidents.

The official analysis<ref name=":1" /> confirms this apparent crime rise was predominantly the statistical effect of improved police recording practices, recovering the historical backlog identified by HMICFRS. Further supporting this conclusion is the finding that when violence with and without injury offences (the categories most affected by under-recording) are removed from both series, the police-recorded crime trends show similarity with the CSEW trends. This indicates that the majority of the apparent surge in crime figures during this decade was concentrated in the statistical recovery of historically mismanaged, high-harm reports, particularly violence against the person and sexual offences.<ref name=":12" /> It is also thought that growing awareness by the police of what constitutes hate crime has also led to improved identification of such offences by officers. Because of these changes, police recorded crime figures do not provide reliable trends in hate crime from 2014.<ref name=":18" />

In 2017, the CSEW began estimating the prevalence of fraud and computer misuse. This include bank and credit card fraud, advance fee fraud, consumer and retail fraud, and similar offences in addition to ‘unauthorised access to personal information’ (including hacking) and ‘computer viruses’.<ref name=":15" /> The additional data has produced a large increase in the UK's headline crime figure, and in 2022 fraud accounted for 41% of all crimes committed in England and Wales.<ref name=":16">{{Cite web|title=Progress combatting fraud - Committee of Public Accounts|url=https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/cm5803/cmselect/cmpubacc/40/report.html|website=publications.parliament.uk|access-date=2025-11-27|date=2023-03-23}}</ref>

==== 2020 onwards ====
In 2023, the standardisation of the Principal Offence Rule (POR), implemented as part of changes to the Home Office Counting Rules (HOCR), had several effects largely aimed at reducing police bureaucracy and refocusing on the most serious crimes.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-04-13 |title=Police given more time to focus on solving crimes and protecting public |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/news/police-given-more-time-to-focus-on-solving-crimes-and-protecting-public |access-date=2025-11-10 |website=GOV.UK |language=en}}</ref> Before 2018, if a crime of stalking or harassment was involved, this would also be recorded in addition to the most serious crime. The 2023 change reintroduced the principal crime rule for all offences (except for modern slavery offences and passport application fraud).<ref name=":10" /> 

The POR means that when a victim reports a single incident that involves multiple different crimes, police now only record the 'principal offence,' which is defined as the crime with the most significant impact on the victim. In addition, there is the Finished Incident Rule in the HOCR. This rule states that:

'''an incident comprising a sequence of crimes between the same offender (or group of offenders) and the same victim should be counted as one crime if reported to the police all at once''<nowiki/>'.

However, in Scotland, where individual dates and times are known or where a different location of the same crime is identified, separate crimes will be recorded.<ref name=":3" />

The effects of these changes raised significant concerns, particularly from the [[Domestic Abuse Commissioner]], that the rules masked the true extent and nature of repeated or multiple offences. This is especially true in cases like domestic abuse, which often involve a series of crimes (e.g., harassment, [[common assault]], criminal damage) during a single incident.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |date=2024-01-25 |title=Distorted police statistics downplay domestic abuse reports, says Commissioner |url=https://domesticabusecommissioner.uk/distorted-police-statistics-downplay-domestic-abuse-reports-says-commissioner/ |access-date=2025-11-10 |website=Domestic Abuse Commissioner |language=en-GB}}</ref> For example, the [[Office for National Statistics]] noted a 6.6% decrease compared with the previous year in domestic abuse-related crimes in England and Wales for the year ending March 2024.<ref name=":5" />

In 2024, the [[Office for Statistics Regulation]] published a review of findings regarding the quality of police statistics following their withdrawal of accreditation in 2014. They found a positive shift in the culture around crime recording, with forces appearing to take crime data integrity seriously, and being more committed to ensuring it met national standards. However, challenges remained relating to the complexity of reporting and frequency of changes made to it, with some reports of over-counting out of caution that a force might be found to be in breach of the rules.<ref name=":10">{{Cite web |date=2024-05-16 |title=The quality of police recorded crime statistics for England and Wales |url=https://osr.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/publication/the-quality-of-police-recorded-crime-statistics-for-england-and-wales/ |access-date=2025-11-10 |website=Office for Statistics Regulation |language=en-GB}}</ref>
[[File:Home Secretary James Cleverly hosts the Global Fraud Summit in London on 11 March 2024 - 15.jpg|alt=Photo of delegates standing for commemorative photo on grand staircase.|thumb|UK [[Home Secretary]] [[James Cleverly]] hosts the first Global Fraud Summit at [[Lancaster House]], London November 2024.]]
Following widespread criticisms of the performance of the [[National Fraud Intelligence Bureau]]'s (NFIB) [[Action Fraud]] service<ref name=":16" /> the [[City of London Police]] has replaced this with [[National Fraud Intelligence Bureau|Report Fraud]] in 2025.<ref name=":20" /> This £212 million transformation programme<ref>{{Cite web|title=As fraud surges, UK prepares to replace its broken reporting service|url=https://therecord.media/uk-action-fraud-replacement-report-fraud|website=therecord.media|access-date=2025-11-27|language=en|date=2025-09-26}}</ref> is expected to 'significantly impact' the way fraud and computer misuse crimes are recorded and how data quality is managed. Given that this new implementation is a multi-year programme requiring cooperation between the [[Office for National Statistics|ONS]], [[Home Office]], and police forces to understand its impact, it is expected that there will be challenges with the coherence of data sources relating to cyber crime.<ref name=":15">{{Cite web |date=2025-04-03 |title=Review of fraud and computer misuse statistics for England and Wales |url=https://osr.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/publication/review-of-fraud-and-computer-misuse-statistics-for-england-and-wales/ |access-date=2025-11-10 |website=Office for Statistics Regulation |language=en-GB}}</ref> {{As of|2023}}, fraud is estimated to comprise about 40% of all crime reported in the UK.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fraud and the Justice System - Justice Committee |url=https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/cm5803/cmselect/cmjust/12/report.html |access-date=2025-12-13 |website=publications.parliament.uk}}</ref>

=== Wider effects of changes ===

==== Outcome rates and detection ====
<!-- PLEASE NOTE: Content in this section is {{excerpt}}ed by "Law enforcement in the United Kingdom##Capacity to solve crimes". See TM:HIDDENEXCERPTADVICE. -->
From 2015, police forces have published monthly 'positive outcome' rates<ref>{{Cite web |title=MPS overview of crimes |url=https://public.tableau.com/app/profile/metropolitan.police.service/viz/MonthlyCrimeDataNewCats/Coversheet |access-date=2025-11-21 |website=Monthly Crime Data New Cats}}</ref> (a somewhat wider definition from the previous 'sanction detection' rates) for offenders receiving some formal sanction such as being charged or summonsed.<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |title=Crime outcomes in England and Wales: Technical annex |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/crime-outcomes-in-england-and-wales-2023-to-2024/crime-outcomes-in-england-and-wales-technical-annex |access-date=2025-11-21 |website=GOV.UK |language=en}}</ref> These include charges, but also outcomes such as Penalty Notices for Disorder (PNDs), warnings for cannabis possession, offences that are asked to be taken into consideration by a court (TICs), cautions, and other warnings and reprimands.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Crimes detected in England and Wales 2010 to 2011 |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/crimes-detected-in-england-and-wales-2010-to-2011 |access-date=2025-11-21 |website=GOV.UK |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":9" />

Nationally, detection rates have been falling as police-reported crime has been rising.<ref name=":02">{{Cite web |date=2019-01-13 |title=A policing paradox: As crime rises, detection rates of those responsible fall |url=https://policinginsight.com/feature/analysis/a-policing-paradox-as-crime-rises-detection-rates-of-those-responsible-fall/ |access-date=2025-11-21 |website=Policing Insight |language=en}}</ref> In 2024, there was even a zero detection rate for crimes within 166 neighborhood areas under the responsibility of the [[Metropolitan Police|Metropolitan Police Service]] (MPS).<ref name="a479">{{cite web |last=Martin |first=Amy-Clare |date=2024-07-15 |title=Met Police failed to solve any neighbourhood crimes in more than 160 areas in 3 years |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/crime/met-police-neighbourhood-crime-dispatches-b2580025.html |access-date=2025-02-19 |website=The Independent}}</ref><ref name="p290">{{cite web |last=Reporters |first=Telegraph |date=2024-07-15 |title=Met fails to identify a single burglary suspect in more than 150 neighbourhoods for three years |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/07/15/met-police-burglary-suspect-failure-identify-channel-4-disp/ |access-date=2025-02-19 |website=The Telegraph}}</ref> More generally, positive outcome rates for the MPS were just 7.3% on average, with some crimes (criminal damage and offences against vehicles) as low as 0.9% in 2022/2023, while drug offences had a 38% detection rate.<ref name="w3842">{{Cite web |title=2022 - 2023 crime statistics {{!}} Metropolitan Police |url=https://www.met.police.uk/police-forces/metropolitan-police/areas/stats-and-data/stats-and-data/met/year-end-crime-statistics-22-23/?_t_id=-6IHkVpPtbGFgCawtQ1uDg==&_t_uuid=9Tkz63K9QxCij2UOAm1IKw&_t_q=crime-statistics-22-23&_t_tags=siteid:9a7e26e6-9ba2-42bf-80ec-103507e5aec9,language:en,and querymatch&_t_hit.id=Cds_Soh_Web_Models_Pages_StatsAndData/_141c69b7-ced9-4199-a0f2-8b486032ff0d_en-GB&_t_hit.pos=4 |access-date=2025-11-20 |website=www.met.police.uk}}</ref> Corresponding figures for 2010/2011 were far higher, with an average total of 24%.<ref>Home Office (July 2011). [http://www.homeoffice.gov.uk/publications/science-research-statistics/research-statistics/crime-research/hosb1111/ Crimes detected in England and Wales 2010/11] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111007163442/http://www.homeoffice.gov.uk/publications/science-research-statistics/research-statistics/crime-research/hosb1111/|date=7 October 2011}}. See Excel file for "Police force area tables".</ref>

However, an increase in crimes reported means the same volume of detections is therefore divided by a much larger number of total recorded offences. While this does not fully explain the drop in detection rates, it is thought to have contributed to it. Other reasons include lack of police resources<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019-12-19 |title=London Assembly - Sanction Detection Rates |url=https://www.london.gov.uk/who-we-are/what-london-assembly-does/questions-mayor/find-an-answer/sanction-detection-rates-7 |website=london.gov.uk}}</ref> and that the crimes the police record disproportionately affect those offences which (in law, if not by the public) are treated as the least serious.<ref name=":02" />

==== In the media ====
From 1998 and particularly from 2002, the impact of the changes were followed by regular reports in the media about rising crime,<ref name=":11">{{Cite web |date=2024-05-23 |title=Most crime has fallen by 90% in 30 years – so why does the public think it’s increased? |url=https://policinginsight.com/feature/analysis/most-crime-has-fallen-by-90-in-30-years-so-why-does-the-public-think-its-increased/ |access-date=2025-11-22 |website=Policing Insight |language=en}}</ref> particularly in terms of figures for 'violence against the person'.{{refn|List of media articles covering rises in crime rates:<ref>{{cite news |date=18 July 2000 |title=BBC 18/07/00 Violent Crime Figures Not Accurate |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/uk/839034.stm |accessdate=13 December 2011 |work=BBC News}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=19 July 2001 |title=BBC 19/07/01 Violent Crime on the rise |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/uk/1447124.stm |accessdate=13 December 2011 |work=BBC News}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Shaw |first=Danny |date=17 July 2003 |title=BBC 17/07/03 Crime figures paint confusing picture |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/uk/3074501.stm |accessdate=13 December 2011 |work=BBC News}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=22 January 2004 |title=BBC 22/01/04 Violent crime up by 14% |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/uk/3419401.stm |accessdate=13 December 2011 |work=BBC News}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=21 April 2005 |title=BBC 21/04/05 Violent Crime Rise Sparks Row |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/uk_politics/vote_2005/frontpage/4467569.stm |accessdate=13 December 2011 |work=BBC News}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Edgington |first1=Tom |date=2018 |title=Reality Check: Are England and Wales experiencing a crime wave? |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-44397532 |access-date=6 November 2018 |work=BBC News |publisher=BBC}}</ref>}} Responding to growing public concern, [[Home Secretary]] [[Sajid Javid]] called on the Government to convene an urgent [[COBR]] meeting to discuss the 'national emergency' in serious violence. However, there were concerns that sensationalised media coverage and political rhetoric had failed to take account of the methodological issues that had produced the rises.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Esposti |first=M. D. |last2=Humphreys |first2=David K. |date=2019-03-21 |title=Media coverage of the "violence epidemic" in England and Wales: are we adding fuel to the fire? |url=https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Media-coverage-of-the-%E2%80%9Cviolence-epidemic%E2%80%9D-in-and-we-Esposti-Humphreys/64db6aa09807eb8fd92e0258587b3306e3439ebb |journal=The British Medical Journal |via=Semantic Scholar}}</ref>

==== International comparisons ====
The UK's reporting standards are not the same as those in other countries, making international comparisons for most crimes problematic. One example is data from the [[United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime]] (UNODC) showing the rate of rape per 100,000 population in England and Wales between 2012 and 2022 increasing from 28.95 to 117.30 (~305%), sexual assault from 39.54 to 125.88 (~218%), and sexual violence from 81.53 to 324.79 (~298%).<ref name="UNODC">{{cite web |title=Violent offences |url=https://dataunodc.un.org/crime-violent-offences |access-date=13 January 2025 |website=dataUNODC |publisher=United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime}}</ref> These figures were almost double the crime rate of the next highest country in those categories among all UN member states in the European region. However, the UNODC frequently cautions that comparisons of recorded crime rates (especially for non-fatal crimes like assault) are heavily affected by different national legal definitions and varying counting and recording rules.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |title=Compiling and Comparing International Crime Statistics |url=https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/data-and-analysis/Compiling-and-comparing-International-Crime-Statistics.html |access-date=2025-11-03 |website=United Nations : Office on Drugs and Crime |language=en}}</ref>

== Declining rates of crime since 1995 ==
{{Main|Crime drop}}

After initial rises in compiled crime data seen by the [[Office for National Statistics]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Crime in England and Wales: Appendix tables - Office for National Statistics |url=https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/crimeandjustice/datasets/crimeinenglandandwalesappendixtables |access-date=2025-11-26 |website=www.ons.gov.uk}}</ref> from the [[Crime Survey for England and Wales]] (CSEW) starting from 1981, trends in most crime began to go steadily downward from 1995. All high-income countries have experienced similar trends. There is scientific consensus that the decline in crime is driven by various factors including better [[physical security]], new technology such as CCTV and tracking methods, and perhaps even [[Lead–crime hypothesis|environmental factors]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Farrell |first=Graham |last2=Davies |first2=Toby |date=2024-05-13 |title=Most crime has fallen by 90% in 30 years – so why does the public think it’s increased? |url=http://theconversation.com/most-crime-has-fallen-by-90-in-30-years-so-why-does-the-public-think-its-increased-228797 |access-date=2025-11-26 |website=The Conversation |language=en-US}}</ref>

Despite this, {{As of|2025|pre=as of late|bare=yes}} over 65% of Britons surveyed think the rate of crime has gone up over time.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-11-17 |title=Crime rate nationally |url=https://yougov.co.uk/topics/politics/trackers/crime-rate-nationally |access-date=2025-11-27 |website=YouGov |language=en-gb}}</ref> Possible reasons for this include media sensationalisation and political rhetoric about emotive but correspondingly rare crimes such as stabbings, terrorism and murder.<ref name=":11" />

As UK crime and law enforcement evolve, changes in reporting methods and systems are ongoing.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wilsher |first1=Roy |title=How effectively do the police record crime? |journal=Report |date=28 August 2025 |url=https://hmicfrs.justiceinspectorates.gov.uk/publication-html/how-effectively-do-the-police-record-crime/ |access-date=12 January 2026 |publisher=His Majesty’s Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services}}</ref> This table lists key events in the history of Police Recorded Crime (PRC) in England and Wales from 1998 to the present.

|style=vertical-align:top |Significant surge in recorded crime, estimated to recover 1 in 5 previously unrecorded offences.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-09-05 |title=Crime and justice methodology |url=https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/crimeandjustice/methodologies/crimeandjusticemethodology |access-date=2025-11-08 |website=Office for National Statistics}}</ref>

|style=vertical-align:top |Causes complex shifts: domestic abuse crimes decreased (-6.6% YE March 2024), while Stalking/Harassment increased.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |date=2024-11-27 |title=Domestic abuse and the criminal justice system, England and Wales: November 2024 |url=https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/crimeandjustice/articles/domesticabuseandthecriminaljusticesystemenglandandwales/november2024 |access-date=2025-11-08 |website=Office for National Statistics}}</ref>

== Comparative reliability of offence types ==
While the [[Crime Survey for England and Wales]] (CSEW) is regarded as the best source of crime trends over the long term, it is not recommended for the comparison of some crime types, particularly high-harm offences which do not occur enough to be covered properly by a victim survey . The [[Office for National Statistics|ONS]] gives the reliability of trend data for each crime type, classed as 'good', 'moderate' or 'poor',<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-11-30 |title=Research outputs: developing a Crime Severity Score for England and Wales using data on crimes recorded by the police |url=https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/crimeandjustice/articles/researchoutputsdevelopingacrimeseverityscoreforenglandandwalesusingdataoncrimesrecordedbythepolice/2016-11-29 |access-date=2025-11-23 |website=Office for National Statistics}}</ref> together with the preferred source. However, with the exception of homicide, the strength of police recorded (PRC) sources should also be taken into account when making comparisons over time.<ref name=":19">{{Cite web |date=2025-11-05 |title=User guide to crime statistics for England and Wales: Offense types |url=https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/crimeandjustice/methodologies/userguidetocrimestatisticsforenglandandwales#offence-types |access-date=2025-11-23 |website=Office of National Statistics}}</ref>
